lessons.subject: literature
lessons.lesson_title: Central idea, evidence, and author's purpose
lessons.previous_learning: September 8 literature work showed stronger theme, inference, and objective summary in fiction.
lessons.course_context: Switch to informational reading and apply the same evidence discipline to central idea and author's purpose.
learning_objectives: Identify evidence that directly supports the central idea.
lessons.why_it_matters: Strong readers explain not only what a text says but which details prove its main idea and why the author included them.

vocabulary.definition: the main point an informational text develops
details that explain or prove the central idea
an additional component or backup that can take over if one part fails
a place where one failure could stop the whole system

lessons.written_instruction:
A backup is not always something that sits unused. In many systems, a backup is part of the design. Engineers call this redundancy: including an extra component, route, or method so that one failure does not automatically stop the entire system.

Consider a building with one staircase. If that staircase becomes blocked, everyone depends on the same path. A building with multiple safe exits has more than one route. The extra route does not guarantee that every emergency will be easy, but it reduces the risk that one blocked path becomes the only option.

Computer systems use similar ideas. Important data may be copied to more than one storage location. Networks may have alternate routes for information. Hospitals may have backup electrical power for critical equipment. In each case, the goal is not to create unnecessary duplication. The goal is to reduce a single failure point.

Redundancy also has costs. Extra equipment can cost money, require maintenance, or make a system more complicated. Good design therefore asks two questions: How serious would a failure be, and how much protection is reasonable?

The important idea is that reliability often comes from planning for failure rather than pretending failure will never happen. A strong system can continue operating, recover more quickly, or fail more safely because another option already exists.

independent_practice.prompt: What is the TOPIC of the article? Answer in 2-5 words.
State the CENTRAL IDEA in one complete sentence.
According to the article, what is redundancy?
Give TWO examples of redundancy from the article.
Explain how multiple safe exits reduce a single failure point.
Why does the author mention costs and maintenance?
What is the author's main purpose: entertain, persuade, or explain? Defend your choice with evidence.

exit_ticket.prompt: Choose one detail from the article and explain exactly how it supports the central idea.
exit_ticket.answer: Answers vary; the explanation must connect a specific redundancy example to reducing single failure points or improving reliability.

lessons.voice_prompt: Switch from fiction to informational reading. Do not tell Atticus the central idea before he reads. Distinguish topic from central idea and evidence from merely interesting details. After an evidence answer, ask briefly: 'What does that prove?' Do not supply assigned answers.
